      Abstract
We study invertibility of λ-terms modulo λ-theories. Here a fundamental role is played by a class
of λ-terms called finite hereditary permutations (FHP) and by their infinite generalisations (HP).
More precisely, FHPs are the invertible elements in the least extensional λ-theory λη and HPs are
those in the greatest sensible λ-theory H∗ . Our approach is based on inverse semigroups, algebraic
structures that generalise groups and semilattices. We show that FHP modulo a λ-theory T is always
an inverse semigroup and that HP modulo T is an inverse semigroup whenever T contains the theory
of Böhm trees. An inverse semigroup comes equipped with a natural order. We prove that the
natural order corresponds to η-expansion in FHP/T, and to infinite η-expansion in HP/T. Building
on these correspondences we obtain the two main contributions of this work: firstly, we recast in
a broader framework the results cited at the beginning; secondly, we prove that the FHPs are the
invertible λ-terms in all the λ-theories lying between λη and H+ . The latter is Morris’ observational
λ-theory, defined by using the β-normal forms as observables.

 1      Introduction
The λ-calculus, established by Alonzo Church in the 1930s, has played a prominent role in
theoretical computer science for almost a century [6, 5, 7]. This stems from its position at
the crossroads of programming language theory and various branches of mathematics, which
draws the attention of a diverse community of researchers. Its denotational semantics has
been studied using domain theory [2], category theory [40, 3] and bicategory theory [29, 37],
game semantics [26, 9, 13], linear logic [1, 22], set theory [39, 21], and universal algebra [45].
Operational aspects of its semantics have been also mechanised in proof assistants [16, 41].
    This article fits within the line of research that studies the λ-calculus from an algebraic
perspective. In [12], Church formulated the λ-calculus as a semigroup where M ◦ N =
λx.M (N x), whence its connection with algebra begins at the syntactic level, and this
perspective also inspired subsequent works [11]. A problem that naturally arises is the
characterisation of those λ-terms M that are invertible in the sense that M ◦ N = N ◦ M = I
(the identity), for some N . The set of invertible λ-terms modulo a λ-theory is a group.
When the notion of equality is =β the group is trivial, as the only invertible λ-term is I.
The problem becomes more interesting when considering extensional λ-theories: Dezani-
Ciancaglini, Bergstra and Klop have characterised the λ-terms invertible modulo =βη as
the finite hereditary permutations (FHPs) [20, 8]. Intuitively, FHPs are obtained from η-

      that they are the only realisers of type isomorphisms in the simply typed λ-calculus [15]. The
      invertibility modulo =βη has also been studied by Folkerts [23], who proved that a λ-term is
      invertible if and only if it is both injective and surjective–a property that seems natural but
      fails in other λ-theories. More recently, Statman has shown that the semigroup of λ-terms
      modulo =β is Sq-universal [49], a profound result stating that every countable semigroup is
      embeddable in the semigroup of λ-terms modulo a suitable λ-theory.
          There are other λ-theories that are of interest for computer scientists because they capture
      operational properties of programs. In particular, Morris defined observational equivalences
      where two λ-terms are equivalent if they display the same behaviour when they are plugged
      in any context [46]. Clearly, this notion depends on the behavioural property one decides
      to observe. The observational equivalence H∗ , where one observes head termination, is by
      far the most studied λ-theory: it arises as the theory of Scott’s model D∞ and captures
      the Böhm tree equality modulo an infinitary notion of extensionality [32]. In [8], Bergstra
      and Klop characterised the class of invertible λ-terms modulo H∗ by generalising the finite
      hereditary permutations to permutations having a possibly infinite Böhm tree (HPs).
          It is natural to consider the problem of characterising invertibility modulo λ-theories lying
      between =βη and H∗ ; one of these is for instance H+ , Morris’s observational theory in which
      the observed behavioural property is β-normalisation [34]. In this paper, we aim to advance
      the study of this problem by extending the results presented in [6, Chapter 21]. Our novel
      approach consists in showing that HP, which is a monoid modulo =β and a group modulo H∗ ,
      is an inverse semigroup (actually, an inverse monoid) modulo the λ-theory of Böhm trees. An
      inverse semigroup [42] is a semigroup in which every element admits a unique inverse in the
      generalised sense of semigroup theory. By virtue of their rich structure, inverse semigroups
      are connected with various areas of logic and theoretical computer science, including topos
      theory [24, 25], Stone duality [43], and automata theory [17]. They simultaneously and
      faithfully generalise groups–since they are equipped with a unary operation extending the
      group inverse–and semilattices, as the idempotent elements of an inverse semigroup always
      form a semilattice with respect to a natural order. An inverse semigroup is a semilattice if
      and only if every element is idempotent, and it is a group if and only if the identity is the only
      idempotent. The prototypical example of an inverse monoid is given by the injective partial
      endofunctions on a set; viewed in this way, inverse monoids provide a natural framework for
      describing partial symmetries, as opposed to the total ones described by groups.
          We introduce a new monoid whose elements we call permutation trees, which can be put
      into correspondence with a monoid of Böhm-like trees. We show that the permutation trees
      form an inverse monoid, we characterise its idempotents and the associated order, and we
      prove that it is in fact F -inverse, a technical concept that will be appropriately explained.
      The analysis of this monoid has two important consequences: HP modulo Böhm tree equality
      and FHP modulo =β form inverse monoids; these sets remain so when considered modulo
      any theory extending Böhm tree equality and =β , respectively. A noteworthy aspect is
      that the natural order on these inverse monoids coincides with the preorder induced by
      infinite η-expansion (on Böhm-like trees) and finite η-expansion (on λ-terms). Quotienting
      an inverse monoid by a suitable congruence σ, called minimum group congruence, yields a
      group in which all idempotents lie in the equivalence class of the identity. In this group, the
      generalised inverses become actual inverses in the usual group-theoretic sense. This naturally
      raises the question of what such a congruence corresponds to in the cases of HP modulo
      Böhm tree equality and FHP modulo =β . The minimum group congruence is related to the
      natural order that corresponds to infinite η-expansion in the theory of Böhm trees and to

theory and then by σ gives precisely HP modulo H∗ ; similarly, quotienting FHP by =β and
then by σ gives precisely FHP modulo =βη . This provides a new perspective on invertible

    The λ-theories H∗ and =βη are special in that they arise precisely from the minimum
group congruence, but this is not always the case. A counterexample is given by the theory
H+ , whose equality has been characterised in terms of the interaction between Böhm trees
and finite η-expansions [14, 47, 34]. To characterise when two hereditary permutations are
equal in H+ , we therefore need to take a further step and study the interaction between
infinite trees equipped with an order that nonetheless originates from finite idempotents. In
other words, we are led to consider a congruence inspired by, but distinct from, the minimum
group congruence. In the theory of Böhm trees, the order constructed in this way coincides
with finite η-expansion. Building on the characterisation of the invertibles we gave for H∗ , we
demonstrate that the λ-terms invertible modulo H+ are precisely FHPs. As a consequence,
FHPs are the invertible λ-terms in all the λ-theories lying between =βη and H+ . This
result settles a conjecture formulated by Barendregt in his book [6, p. 547]. The conceptual
reconstruction of invertibles modulo H∗ and =βη together with the characterisation of
invertibles modulo H+ constitute the main contributions of this work. Some directions for
future research are outlined in the conclusion.


 2      Preliminaries
We recall some basic notions and results concerning the λ-calculus and the theory of
semigroups. We refer to [6, 7] for the former, and to [31, 42] for the latter.
    We denote by N the set of natural numbers and by N+ the set of positive natural numbers.
For every n ∈ N, let Sn be the symmetric group on n elements. Let Sym(N+ ) be the
symmetric group on N+ . For every n ≥ 1, Sn can be embedded in Sym(N+ ) as the subgroup
of all the ρ ∈ Sym(N+ ) such that ρi = i for all i > n. By abuse of notation, we shall write
Sn for the image of this embedding. We denote by ι the identity permutation in Sym(N+ ).

2.1     Inverse semigroups
Given a semigroup S, we say that u ∈ S is regular if there is v ∈ S such that uvu = u. A
semigroup is called regular if every element is regular. Moreover, we say that v is an inverse
of u if uvu = u and vuv = v. Every element in a regular semigroup admits at least on inverse.
An extremely important class of regular semigroups is that of inverse semigroups, in which
every element admits precisely one inverse.

▶ Definition 1. An inverse semigroup is a semigroup S endowed with a unary operation
(−)∗ that satisfies, for all u, v ∈ S:

     (u∗ )∗ = u,   (uv)∗ = v ∗ u∗ ,    uu∗ u = u,      uu∗ vv ∗ = vv ∗ uu∗ .                (1)

An inverse monoid is an inverse semigroup together with a unit for multiplication.

In an inverse semigroup u∗ is the unique inverse of u.

▶ Example 2. The prototypical example of an inverse monoid is the set I(X) of partial
injections on a given set X. An element u is a bijection between two subsets of X, the
domain and the range of u, and u∗ is its partial inverse.

2.2    Trees
An ordered tree is a non-empty subset A of (N+ )∗ such that:
 (i) A is closed under initial segments;
 (ii) A is gapless: for every i, j ∈ N+ and every w ∈ A, if i < j and wj ∈ A, then wi ∈ A.
The elements of A are called nodes; a node is a leaf if it has no children (immediate successors).
The empty word ϵ is the unique root, i.e., node without immediate predecessors. We will be
exclusively interested in finitely branching trees, i.e., trees whose nodes have a finite number
of children. We denote by rd(A) the degree of the root of A, i.e., the number of its children.
For each 1 ≤ i ≤ rd(A) we denote by Ai := {w ∈ (N+ )∗ : iw ∈ A} the subtree of A of root i.
Finally, we say that a labelled tree is a function l : A → L from a tree to a nonempty set L
of labels. The tree A is called the skeleton of l, and is denoted by sk(l).
    The set of finitely branching ordered trees can be defined coinductively. When we deal
with infinite trees we will freely use coinductive arguments. We refer the reader to [38] for a
gentle introduction to coinductive techniques.


2.3    Lambda calculus
The set Λ of λ-terms over a countably infinite set Var of variables is defined by the grammar:

   M, N ::= x | λx.M | M N, for x ∈ Var.

We assume that application associates on the left, and has higher precedence than abstraction.
For instance, λxyz.xyz stands for λx.(λy.(λz.(xy)z)). From now on, λ-terms are considered
up to renaming of bound variables. A λ-term without free variables is called a combinator.
The β-reduction →β and η-reduction →η are defined as the contextual closures of the rules:

   (λx.M )N →β M [N/x],               λx.M x →η M, if x does not occur free in M

where we denote by M [N/x] the capture-free substitution of N for all free occurrences of
x in M . Given a notion of reduction →r between λ-terms, we denote by ↠r the reflexive,
transitive closure of →r , and by =r the least equivalence relation containing →r . When
→r is confluent, nf r (M ) stands for the unique r-normal form of M (if any). We define
βη-reduction as →βη = →β ∪ →η . The combinators below are used throughout the paper:

   I = λx.x,      1 = λxy.xy,        B = λf gx.f (gx),      Y = λf.(λx.f (xx))(λx.f (xx)).

We recall that I is the identity, 1 the 1st Church numeral, B stands for the composition and
Y is Curry’s fixed point combinator satisfying YM =β M (YM ), for every M ∈ Λ.

       3       Permutation trees
      In this section we introduce and study a new inverse monoid PT of labelled ordered trees,
      that, as shown in Proposition 17, is isomorphic to the monoid of hereditary permutations
      (HP, ◦, I). Working with PT has the advantage of revealing the underlying structure in a
      more transparent way.

      ▶ Definition 12. A permutation tree is a labelled ordered tree t : A → Sym(N+ ) such that:
         if a ∈ A has exactly n ≥ 1 children, then t(a) ∈ Sn ;
         if a ∈ A is a leaf, then t(a) := ι, where ι is the identity permutation in Sym(N+ ).
      We let PT be the set of permutation trees.

         We denote by ϵ̄ the unique permutation tree with skeleton {ϵ}, i.e. the tree with one node
      labelled ι.
         We can conveniently write a permutation tree t as ⟨π; t1 , . . . , tn ⟩ where π ∈ Sn is the
      label of the root, rd(t) = n and t1 , . . . , tn ∈ PT.
         Observe that PT can be defined coinductively as the greatest set PT such that, if t ∈ PT,
      then there is n ∈ N, π ∈ Sn and t1 , . . . , tn ∈ PT such that t = ⟨π; t1 , . . . , tn ⟩.

      ▶ Definition 13. Let t, u ∈ PT. We define the product tu by coinduction as follows. First,
      tϵ̄ = t = ϵ̄t. If t = ⟨π; t1 , . . . , tn ⟩, u = ⟨ρ; u1 , . . . , um ⟩ and k = max{n, m}, then we define:

           tu := ⟨π ◦ ρ; u1 tρ1 , . . . , uk tρk ⟩

      where, by convention, tj = ϵ̄ if j > n, and ui = ϵ̄ if i > m.

         The product operation makes (PT, ·, ϵ̄) into a monoid. We now show that this monoid is
      an inverse monoid.

      ▶ Definition 14. Given t ∈ PT, we define by coinduction t∗ as follows. First, ϵ̄∗ = ϵ̄. If
      t = ⟨π; t1 , . . . , tn ⟩ with n ≥ 1, then t∗ = ⟨π −1 ; (tπ−1 1 )∗ , . . . , (tπ−1 n )∗ ⟩.

         We denote by E the set {t ∈ PT : t(a) = ι for every a ∈ sk(t)}. Every t ∈ E is univocally
      determined by its skeleton and we identify sk(t) with the permutation tree t.

 5     Related and further work
Inverse semigroups were first employed in the λ-calculus to study properties of β-reduction [18].
Subsequently, they played a role in Girard’s Geometry of Interaction [27]. More recently,
Goubault-Larrecq, inspired by the work [18, 19], has shown that a category constructed from
an inverse semigroup models a fragment of linear logic [28]. Hofmann and Mislove employed
the theory of inverse semigroups to prove that every compact Hausdorff topological model of
λ-calculus is degenerate [30]. We have shown that the theory of inverse semigroups improves
our understanding of the interaction between invertible and idempotent elements, which is
essential for characterising λ-terms invertible modulo λ-theories. Looking ahead, we aim
to characterise elements that are invertible modulo λ-theories lying strictly between H+
and H∗ . The role played by E and Efin in H∗ and H+ , respectively, is taken on by other
well-behaved semilattices of idempotents of PT. We conjecture that there exist λ-theories
between H+ and H∗ whose group of invertible elements is strictly between FHP and HP.
